name: Bigthan and Teresh
charge: Conspiring to lay hands on king Ahasuerus
summary: Two chamberlains who kept the door were wroth and sought to lay hand on the king. Mordecai heard of it and told Esther, who told the king in Mordecai's name. They were hanged, and the thing was written in the chronicles, where a sleepless king found it years later on the night before Haman meant to hang Mordecai.
offense: Bigthan and Teresh were chamberlains entrusted with keeping the door. In their anger they sought to lay hands on Ahasuerus. Access given for the king's protection became an opportunity for a plot against his life (Esther 2:21). Mordecai learned of it and told Esther, who reported it to the king in Mordecai's name. The accusation was investigated and found true. The sequence distinguishes a discovered plot from a sentence resting upon an unexamined report (Esther 2:22-23).
judgment: Both conspirators were hanged on a tree, and the matter was entered in the royal chronicles. Mordecai's service received no immediate reward, but the written record preserved his part in saving the king. Later, during a sleepless night, Ahasuerus heard that record read and asked what honor Mordecai had received. Haman arrived intending to request Mordecai's death and instead was commanded to honor him (Esther 6:1-11). The record of one defeated conspiracy helped overturn another. A service apparently forgotten remained available at the moment its remembrance would matter.

verses.text: In those days, while Mordecai sat in the king’s gate, two of the king’s chamberlains, Bigthan and Teresh, of those which kept the door, were wroth, and sought to lay hand on the king Ahasuerus.
And the thing was known to Mordecai, who told it unto Esther the queen; and Esther certified the king thereof in Mordecai’s name.
And when inquisition was made of the matter, it was found out; therefore they were both hanged on a tree: and it was written in the book of the chronicles before the king.
On that night could not the king sleep, and he commanded to bring the book of records of the chronicles; and they were read before the king.
And it was found written, that Mordecai had told of Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king’s chamberlains, the keepers of the door, who sought to lay hand on the king Ahasuerus.
And the king said, What honour and dignity hath been done to Mordecai for this? Then said the king’s servants that ministered unto him, There is nothing done for him.

Then the king said to Haman, Make haste, and take the apparel and the horse, as thou hast said, and do even so to Mordecai the Jew, that sitteth at the king’s gate: let nothing fail of all that thou hast spoken.

Then took Haman the apparel and the horse, and arrayed Mordecai, and brought him on horseback through the street of the city, and proclaimed before him, Thus shall it be done unto the man whom the king delighteth to honour.
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God: and they that resist shall receive to themselves damnation.
Curse not the king, no not in thy thought; and curse not the rich in thy bedchamber: for a bird of the air shall carry the voice, and that which hath wings shall tell the matter.

entries.commentary: After the wrath of king Ahasuerus was appeased he remembered Vashti and what she had done and what was decreed against her. His servants counsel that fair young virgins be sought for the king in every province and gathered to Shushan the palace under the custody of the keeper of the women. Fair young virgins here does not mean little girls but women of marital age, and the maiden who pleased the king would be made queen instead of Vashti, and the thing pleased the king. -

There was a certain Jew in Shushan named Mordecai, son of Jair, a Benjamite carried away from Jerusalem with the captivity taken with Jeconiah king of Judah whom Nebuchadnezzar carried away. This gives the lapse of time telling when Mordecai was put into captivity. Mordecai brought up Hadassah, that is Esther, his uncle's daughter, for she had neither father nor mother, and the maid was fair and beautiful, and when her parents were dead he took her for his own daughter. Esther is a Persian name after Ishtar, which is one reason the old rabbis said little of this book.

When the king's commandment was heard and many maidens were gathered to Shushan under Hegai, Esther was brought also to the king's house, and the maiden pleased him and obtained kindness, and he gave her things for purification and seven maidens and preferred her to the best place of the house of the women. Esther had not shown her people nor her kindred, for Mordecai had charged her not to show it, and Mordecai walked every day before the court of the women's house to know how Esther did. She is racially ambiguous, a daughter of Israel who could not be told at a glance to be black or Hispanic, which is why we go by whether a spirit bears witness with this Bible.

Every maid's turn to go in to the king came after twelve months of purification, six months with oil of myrrh and six months with sweet odours and other things for the purifying of the women. Israel kept such a season of preparing, and our women always smelled good. She went in the evening and returned to the second house of the women under the keeper of the concubines, and came in unto the king no more except he delighted in her and called her by name. The king had houses set aside for his concubines, for he was the king of Persia and not an Israelite.

When Esther's turn came, the daughter of Abihail the uncle of Mordecai who took her for his daughter, she required nothing but what Hegai the keeper of the women appointed, and Esther obtained favour in the sight of all who looked upon her. The king loved Esther above all the women, and she obtained grace and favour more than all the virgins, so he set the royal crown upon her head and made her queen instead of Vashti, and made a great feast, Esther's feast, and a release to the provinces with gifts. Esther was chosen above all the women, for that is what a daughter of Israel is.

When the virgins were gathered the second time, Mordecai sat in the king's gate, and Esther had not yet showed her kindred nor her people as Mordecai had charged her. Esther did the commandment of Mordecai just as when she was brought up with him, still subject to her uncle and still listening to him even after she was made queen.

In those days, while Mordecai sat in the king's gate, two of the king's chamberlains that kept the door were wroth and sought to lay hands on king Ahasuerus, plotting a coup against him. The thing was known to Mordecai who told it to Esther the queen, and Esther told the king in Mordecai's name, and when it was searched out and found true the two were both hanged on a tree, and it was written in the book of the chronicles before the king. Israel wrote down our history and our chronicles, and this deed of Mordecai's would later help our whole nation. -

That night the king could not sleep, and he called for the book of records of the chronicles to be read before him. This is how the Most High works, moving even a king's sleeplessness to set His purpose in motion. It was found written that Mordecai had told of Bigthana and Teresh, two chamberlains who sought to lay hand on the king, and yet nothing had been done to honor him for it. The king asked what honor had been done to Mordecai, and his servants answered that there was nothing done for him.

The king asked who was in the court, and Haman had just come into the outer court to speak to the king about hanging Mordecai on the gallows he had prepared. In the previous chapter Haman's wife had told him to make a gallows fifty cubits high and hang Mordecai on it, so Haman was coming to carry out that plan at the very moment the king had learned Mordecai saved his life. The king's servant said Haman stood in the court, and the king called for him to come in.

The king asked Haman what should be done to the man the king delights to honor, and Haman, being so full of himself, assumed the king must mean him, for who in the kingdom was better than he. Haman laid out a full plan of royal apparel the king wears, the horse the king rides, and the crown set upon the head, all delivered by a noble prince to array the man and parade him through the city. Because of his pride Haman designed the highest honor imaginable, thinking he himself would receive it.

The king told Haman to make haste and do exactly as he said to Mordecai the Jew who sat at the king's gate, letting nothing fail of all he had spoken. Haman then took the apparel and the horse, arrayed Mordecai, brought him on horseback through the street, and proclaimed before him. What Haman planned for himself was given to the man he hated. This is how the Most High works, and it should put a smile on your face.

Mordecai returned to the king's gate, but Haman hurried to his house mourning with his head covered, and told his wife Zeresh and his friends all that had happened. His wise men and his wife told him that if Mordecai was of the seed of the Jews, before whom he had begun to fall, he would not prevail but would surely fall before him. While they yet talked, the king's chamberlains came to hasten Haman to the banquet Esther had prepared, the banquet she set up after hearing of the decree against her people.

Dead flies make the apothecary's ointment stink; so a little folly ruins the man who holds a reputation for wisdom and honor. A wise man's heart is at his right hand, but a fool's heart at his left. Even as the fool walks by the way his wisdom fails him, and he shows everyone that he is a fool. If the spirit of the ruler rises against you, leave not your place, for yielding pacifies great offenses.

There is an evil under the sun, an error that proceeds from the ruler: folly is set in high dignity while the rich sit in a low place. He has seen servants riding upon horses and princes walking as servants upon the earth, the natural order turned upside down.

He that digs a pit shall fall into it, and whoever breaks a hedge a serpent shall bite; he that removes stones is hurt by them, and he that cleaves wood is endangered by it. If the iron is blunt and the edge is not whetted, more strength is needed, but wisdom is profitable to direct. The serpent bites without enchantment, and a babbler is no better.

The words of a wise man's mouth are gracious, but the fool is swallowed up by his own lips. His talk begins in foolishness and ends in mischievous madness. A fool is full of words, though no man can tell what shall be after him. The labor of the foolish wearies every one of them because he does not even know how to go to the city.

Woe to the land whose king is a child and whose princes eat in the morning; blessed is the land whose king is the son of nobles and whose princes eat in due season, for strength and not for drunkenness. Slothfulness lets the building decay and idleness makes the house drop through. A feast is made for laughter and wine makes merry, but money answers all things. Curse not the king, not even in your thought, nor the rich in your bedchamber, for a bird of the air shall carry the voice and tell the matter.
